title: Prologue (lines 1–98)

teacherSummary.text: Before dawn after the war, Antigone tells her sister Ismene that King Creon has forbidden anyone to bury their brother Polyneices, who attacked Thebes; Eteocles, who defended it, will be buried with honour. Antigone will bury Polyneices and asks Ismene to help. Ismene, recalling the ruin of their family, refuses: they are women and cannot defy the State. Antigone goes alone.

context.history: For Greeks, leaving a body unburied denied the dead rest and offended the gods. The two brothers had killed each other in the war over Thebes; this play was written before Oedipus Rex and Oedipus at Colonus, though its story comes last.

significance: The sisters embody two answers to an unjust law: open defiance and fearful obedience. Ismene's "weak women" (line 60) states her society's view of women, which Antigone's action challenges.

safeMessaging.teacherScript: In the opening scene Ismene recalls that their father, Oedipus, blinded himself (line 51) and that their mother, Jocasta, took her own life (line 53), part of the curse on their family. Later in the play, three more people take their own lives: Antigone in the tomb, Haemon beside her, and Queen Eurydice when she hears the news. In Greek tragedy such deaths happen offstage and are reported by a messenger. The play does not present them as noble or as a solution. It shows them as the ruin of Creon's house, the result of a pride that would not bend until too late. Hurting yourself is wrong and is never the answer.
